title: The Song of the Last Meeting
text:
My chest was growing cold, helpless,

but my steps were light.

I put on my right hand

the glove from my left hand.


It seemed to me there were many steps,

although I knew there were only three!

An autumn murmur among the maples

asked me: "Die with me!


Listen: a painful,

fickle and wicked fate has deceived me!"

I answered it: "My dear:

me too. I will die with you!"


This is the song of the last meeting.

I cast a glance at the gloomy house.

Only in the bedroom did the candles burn

with an indifferent and withered flame.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the glove mistake, autumn murmur, and indifferent candlelight of the last meeting.

title: Native Land
text:
We do not carry it in dark amulets,

nor write rapturous sighs about it,

it does not disturb our bitter sleep,

nor seem to us the promised paradise.

In our soul we do not turn it

into an object bought or sold.

For it, sick, destitute, wandering,

we do not even remember it.


Yes, for us it is dirt on our shoes.

Yes, for us it is grit between our teeth.

And we grind, tear out, crush

that earth that mixes with nothing.

But in it we lie and we are it,

and therefore, happy, we call it ours.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the unsentimental homeland as dirt, grit, burial ground, and identity.

title: I Grew Up amid a Populated Silence...
text:
I grew up amid a populated silence

inside the cold cradle of the newborn century.

Human voices did not touch me.

It was the voices of the wind I heard.

I gave my favors to burdocks and weeds,

but what was most precious to me was the silver willow,

great companion through the years,

whose weeping branches

quickened my insomnia with dreams.

Unbelievably I have survived:

outside only a severed trunk remains. Now other

willows

recite under our skies

with alienated voices.

And I remain silent, as if I had lost a brother.




1940
editorial_note: The translation preserves the silver willow as companion, survivor, and lost brother.

title: I Arrive at the Poet's House...
text:
I arrive at the poet's house.

A Sunday. Precisely at noon.

The room is large and quiet.

Outside, in the frozen landscape,


a raspberry-colored sun hangs

over cords of blue-gray smoke.

The scrutinizing gaze of my host

silently envelops me.


His eyes are so serene

that one could lose oneself in them forever.

I know I must be careful

not to return his gaze.


But the conversation is what I remember

from that Sunday at noon,

in the poet's broad gray house

near the gates of the Neva¹.




1914


1. Neva: Russian river that crosses the city of Saint Petersburg
editorial_note: This variant keeps the noon visit, Neva footnote, and dangerously serene gaze.

title: Cleopatra
text:
She has already kissed Antony's dead lips,

has wept on her knees before Caesar

and her servants have betrayed her. Darkness falls.

The trumpets of the Roman eagle shriek.


Here comes the last man seized by her beauty,

—such a gallant suitor—with a shamefaced murmur:

"You will have to walk before him, like a slave, in the triumph."

But the slope of her swan neck is calmer

than ever.


Tomorrow they will chain her children. Nothing remains for her

but to drive that fellow mad

and place the black asp, as a merciful separation,

upon her dark breast, with indifferent hand.




1940
editorial_note: The translation keeps Cleopatra's poise between humiliation, threat, and the merciful asp.

title: I Am Not One of Those Who Abandoned the Land
text:
I am not one of those who abandoned the land

to the mercy of enemies.

Their flatteries leave me cold,

my songs are not for them to praise.


But I pity the exiles.

Like that of a deserter, like that of one half-dead,

dark is your road, wanderer;

bitterness infects your foreign bread.


But here, in the half-light of the conflagration,

when hardly one friend remains to know,

we survivors do not give way

before anything, before a single blow.


Surely the reckoning will be made

after this cloud passes,

we are people without tears,

straighter than you... prouder.




1922
editorial_note: The translation preserves the contrast between exile and remaining inside catastrophe.

title: Madness Already Lifts Its Wing
text:
Madness already lifts its wing

to cover half my soul.

That taste of hypnotic wine!

Temptation of the dark valley!


Now everything is clear.

I admit my defeat. The language

of my deliriums in my ear

is the language of a foreigner.


Useless to fall to one's knees

and implore mercy.

Nothing that matters, except my life,

is mine to carry away:

not my son's terrible eyes,

not the chiseled stone flower

of pain, not the day of the storm,

not tribulation in the visiting hour,

not the dear coldness of his hands,

not the agitated shadow in the lime trees,

not the fine singing of the cricket

in the consoling word of departure.




1940
editorial_note: The translation keeps the encroaching madness and the list of losses that cannot be carried away.

title: When the Moon Is a Melon Slice
text:
When the moon is a melon slice in the window

and around it is haze, the door closed and the house enchanted

by the blue branches of wisteria, and in the clay fountain there is cold water

and the snow of the cloth, and a wax candle burns

as in childhood, butterflies buzz

the calm, which does not hear my word, resounds.

Then from the blackness of Rembrandtesque corners something suddenly coils

and hides there at hand, but I do not tremble, nor even become afraid...

Solitude in its nets made me prisoner.

The black cat looks into my soul, like century-old eyes,

and in the mirror my double is perhaps my opposite.

I am going sweetly to sleep, good night, night.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the surreal domestic nocturne and its mirror-double unease.

title: For Many
text:
I am your voice, warmth of your breath,

the reflection of all your faces,

useless is the beating of the useless wing:

I will be with you until the very end.


And for that reason you love me avidly,

with all my sins and weaknesses,

and for that reason you delivered to me without looking

the best of all your sons,

and for that reason you did not ask me

about that son even once,

and you filled with the smoke of praises

my house already forever empty.

And they say it is no longer possible to unite more closely

and that more irreversibly one cannot love...

As the shadow wants to separate from the body,

as the flesh wants to separate from the soul,

so I desire that you forget me.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the collective address and the bitter wish to be forgotten.

title: Tigers in the Garden
text:
Only for your lips my blood is ripe,

with summer obsession

prepared for your kisses,

always faithful to my arms and full of

beauty,

bloodless every night, and each dawn unharmed.


If the woods crackle with hunting and adventure

and the high birds

mock seeing us imprisoned,

do not let your eyes draw the bitterness

of those who have not carried love in their bones.


Stay in my arms, for you have only me,

for the others

hate you, for the heart lies in wait for you

in the warm beats of belly

and temples.


See that there are no gardens beyond this wall,

that it is all a

long forgetting. and if my love tightens around you

you will see an open sky behind

the dark weeping.


1968
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's tense enclosure, bodily pulse, and the promise of sky behind dark weeping.
